title: After Five parameters
$comment: Slider granularity is x-step, never multipleOf - see bathtub's schema. Property order is the panel's reading order: the clock, then the deal, then the score you are building, then the two gates that test it, then how it is drawn. THE TIME OF DAY IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: it would be serialised into every submission and it is not a choice anyone is making. THE OFFICE RENT BASE IS DELIBERATELY NOT A CONTROL: it is $54/sf asking for Manhattan class B and C, it is published, and it lives once in the manifest's economics block. What is a control is the discount between asking and effective, because THAT is the part nobody published.

district.title: District
district.description: Manhattan Community District 1 is the Financial District, Battery Park City, Tribeca and Governors Island. District 5 is Midtown South, which has a very different office stock - newer, deeper, and much more of it. Both are shipped, and the map crops to the one being looked at; 'both' shows the pair and the mile and a half between them, because the edge of a study area is a choice and it helps to see it.

hour.title: Hour of day
hour.description: The day's clock. Agents walk between the subway gateways and the buildings on the measured curves; playing the year holds this clock at its value, and playing this holds the year.

year.title: Year
year.description: The model tests the deal at each of six dates and a building converts at the first one where it clears. Six dates means the model has six opinions about the future and nothing in between them; the scrubber snaps rather than slides, which is honest about that.

agent_count.title: Agents
agent_count.description: How many walkers stand in for the district's day. A sample for the eye, not a census - the counted flows are the same at any setting, and even the maximum is a twelfth of the people the counts say are here.

schedule_source.title: Schedule
x-enum-notes: Times drawn from the MTA origin-destination curves themselves - October 2024 weekdays, counted taps.
Times drawn from four bell curves you shape below. Their defaults are read off the measured curves, so this starts where the data is and moves away from it knowingly.
schedule_source.description: Where an agent's clock comes from.

arrival_median.title: Arrival median
arrival_median.description: When half the morning's arrivals have happened. 08:47 in the measured curve (October 2024 weekdays).

arrival_spread.title: Arrival spread
arrival_spread.description: The width of the morning peak, in hours.

departure_median.title: Departure median
departure_median.description: When half the evening's departures have happened. 17:28 in the measured curve.

departure_spread.title: Departure spread
departure_spread.description: The width of the evening peak, in hours.

conversion_cost_sf.title: Conversion cost
conversion_cost_sf.description: What it costs to turn a square foot of office into a square foot of apartment: new plumbing risers, new windows where the code demands them, and a floor plan that has to reach daylight. An assumption - no published series was verified for it - and the number most worth arguing with, because the whole debate about conversion is really a debate about this figure.

residential_rent.title: Residential rent
residential_rent.description: What the converted apartments let for, per square foot per year. One figure for the whole district, so a basement studio on Water Street and a corner unit forty floors up earn the same. The model turns it into a value with a fixed capitalisation rate, which assumes the way buildings are priced does not change between now and 2050.

office_rent_trend.title: Office rent trend
office_rent_trend.description: How office rent drifts each year from its base. THIS IS THE ONLY THING THAT MAKES TIME PASS IN THIS MODEL. A building converts at the first date the residential deal beats the office income it gives up, so a falling office market is what opens the gate and a rising one holds it shut. The default is a mild decline, which is an assumption and a consequential one - set it to zero and the map stops changing with the year at all, which tells you how much of this story is the office market rather than anything about housing.

office_rent.title: Office rent
x-enum-notes: The published asking rent. Manhattan Class B and C combined, asking - NYC Comptroller, Spotlight: NYC's Office Market, 14 May 2024, CoStar as of 30 April 2024. THE ONLY STOP WITH A SOURCE. B and C are combined at source, so this sandbox does not pretend to separate them. At this stop nothing converts, and the empty map is the finding.
What a landlord collects. Asking rent is a list price; free months and fit-out allowances are not published, so this stop applies a flat 25% discount. Ours, not anyone's.
A building in trouble. A 40% discount, standing for a half-empty Class C building signing short leases. Ours.
Not really Class B. The Comptroller's 5-star figure is roughly $100; this stop stands for a repositioned building at the top of the B/C band. Ours.
office_rent.description: Four named scenario stops, one sourced and three ours. The deal is tested against this rent; the note above says whose number the selected stop is.

cap_rate_office.title: Cap rate, office
cap_rate_office.description: Market convention, not a measurement - no published NYC office cap-rate series was verified. Office and residential used to share one cap rate silently, which scaled both sides of the comparison and very nearly cancelled; setting these two equal reproduces exactly that. Pull them apart to see what the gap between yields does, because that gap is a large part of why anyone converts anything.

cap_rate_residential.title: Cap rate, residential
cap_rate_residential.description: Market convention, not a measurement - no published NYC residential series was verified either. Equal to the office rate by default, which is what the model used to do without saying so.

opex_share.title: Operating cost
opex_share.description: The share of gross rent that goes on running the building before any of it counts as income. Ours, and applied identically to an office tower and to the apartments it becomes, which is convenient rather than true. Market convention, not a measurement - no published NYC series was verified.

min_units_for_conversion_sample.title: Unit floor in the conversion sample
x-enum-notes: 442 filings, 1,366 sf per apartment. No floor at all - every filing that made a business building residential counts, including one-unit oddities reporting a whole tower's floor area against a single apartment.
149 filings, 1,152 sf per apartment. The shipped default - conversions of ten units or more.
59 filings, 907 sf per apartment. Only conversions of fifty units or more count.
min_units_for_conversion_sample.description: Which DOB conversion filings the floor-area-per-apartment figure is measured from. The cut is a judgement and it moves the answer by 40%; only the six measured cuts are offered, because a value between them would be an invention, not a measurement.

w_depth.title: Weight: floorplate depth
w_depth.description: How much the depth from core to window counts. It is the heaviest weight here, and that is a judgement we made, not one anybody published. The proxy is MapPLUTO's BldgDepth halved, which assumes a centred core and a rectangular plate.

w_f2f.title: Weight: floor-to-floor
w_f2f.description: How much ceiling height counts - the room to run new services under a floor and still have a room. The proxy is modelled height divided by storeys, which averages the lobby and the mechanical floors in with the rest.

w_area.title: Weight: floorplate area
w_area.description: How much a small floor counts. The proxy is floor area over storeys.

w_age.title: Weight: age
w_age.description: How much being old counts, standing in for the kind of facade a building has. It used to stand in for structural bay as well, which it does not measure at all; that is now named as a third missing criterion rather than quietly carried here.

convertibility_threshold.title: Convertibility threshold
convertibility_threshold.description: How convertible a building has to be before anyone tries. The score behind it is OURS, not a consultancy's: the weighted sum of the four proxies above, and three of Gensler's published criteria are dropped outright because nothing available measures them. The weights are relative - they are divided by their own total - so what matters is which one you make heaviest. The legend on the map marks where this slider would have to sit for our score to call a quarter of the district convertible, which is the share Gensler published. It is the only place our judgement and theirs can be held up beside each other, and it moves when you move the weights.

incentive_467m.title: 467-m eligibility rules
incentive_467m.description: The state tax exemption for office-to-residential conversion. Its published terms are here - the building must have been at least 90% non-residential, must make six or more units, and must set aside a quarter of them as affordable - but its BENEFIT SCHEDULE is not: the exemption percentage and duration are not in the published FAQ. So it cannot be given a value, and it is modelled as a gate rather than as money. On, only buildings meeting the published tests convert, on the argument developers make that the deal does not close without it. Off, the tests are not applied and no benefit is added either. The difference between the two settings is what the eligibility rules exclude, not what the money is worth.

colour_by.title: Colour by
colour_by.description: What the colour means. "Use" is the one to start with: blue is still office, red has become housing.

added_floors.title: Show added floors
added_floors.description: Where a filing recorded storeys being added, push the roof up by that many. It is the QUANTITY of the change and not its form - no setback, no courtyard, no new envelope, so a building that grew four floors grows a four-floor block. And it only shows for buildings whose record came from the older filing system, because the newer source carries no height figure at all.
